=== Final_ DCC Comments on Interconnection Standards PFP (Project 58481).pdf ===
                                     PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                        §         PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                     §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA 37.0561                   §                   OF TEXAS


                      COMMENTS OF DATA CENTER COALITION


        The Data Center Coalition (DCC) appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments
to the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) regarding Project No. 58481, Rulemaking to
Implement Large Load Interconnection Standards Under PURA §37.0561. DCC values the
Commission's continued engagement with industry stakeholders throughout this rulemaking
process and acknowledges the significant work that has gone into developing the Proposal for
Publication. DCC offers the following comments.

I. The Proposed Rule Continues to Place Undue, Disproportionate, and Overlapping
Financial Requirements on Large Load Customers

        DCC recognizes the Commission's intent in developing this rule is to establish
meaningful interconnection standards that support business development in Texas while
maintaining system reliability. DCC shares these goals and has engaged constructively
throughout this proceeding to help develop a framework that works for both large load customers
and the utilities that serve them. DCC members are committed to paying their full cost of service
and to providing financial assurances that reflect the genuine risks associated with large load
interconnection.

       DCC also acknowledges several areas where the Proposal for Publication reflects
meaningful progress from earlier drafts. The reduction of the per-MW financial security at the
intermediate agreement stage, the inclusion of a CIAC true-up mechanism, and the definition of
competitively sensitive information are all constructive developments that DCC appreciates.
These changes reflect the Commission's responsiveness to stakeholder input and DCC's
continued commitment to working collaboratively toward a workable final rule.

         Notwithstanding this progress, DCC has significant concerns with the proposed rule as
currently drafted. The rule places a disproportionate share of financial risk on large load
customers through a series of overlapping financial requirements whose individual purposes are
not clearly defined and whose cumulative effect has not been fully evaluated. In several
instances, the financial obligations established by the rule function more as fees than as
cost-recovery mechanisms, and they are triggered by timelines that do not reflect the operational
realities of large load project development. DCC urges the Commission to revisit several key



                                                                                                 1
 provisions to ensure that financial commitments are proportionate, transparent, and grounded in
actual utility exposure — consistent with the cost-causation principles that underpin utility
regulation in Texas and that DCC has advocated throughout this proceeding.

        It is also important to note that the financial commitments established by this rule do not
exist in a vacuum. The Commission is simultaneously considering additional financial
requirements on large load customers in related proceedings, including potential minimum
demand charges and revised transmission cost allocation methodologies in Project No. 58484. As
DCC noted in its comments in that proceeding, the cumulative effect of all financial obligations
imposed on large load customers across these proceedings must be evaluated together to ensure
that the aggregate burden is proportionate, justified, and consistent with the Commission's goal
of supporting business development in Texas.1 DCC urges the Commission to keep this broader
regulatory context in mind as it considers the specific provisions discussed below.

        DCC's four principal concerns with the proposed rule are as follows.

1. The Six-Month Milestone Trigger and Mandatory Capacity Reallocation Do Not
Adequately Account for the Realities of Large Load Development

        The non-utilized capacity provision in §(h) establishes a sequence of consequences —
mandatory notification to ERCOT, mandatory capacity reallocation, and financial forfeiture —
triggered by a six-month milestone miss. Not later than 30 days after a large load customer fails
by six months to satisfy a milestone in its phased energization schedule, the interconnecting
TDSP must notify ERCOT of the customer's non-utilized capacity. Within 60 days, the TDSP
must initiate draw-down on the customer's posted financial security for costs incurred, including
equipment that cannot be canceled, construction that has commenced, and services that have
been initiated. Ultimately, a mandatory re-allocation of capacity introduces a potentially
intolerable risk to new large, grid connected, load in Texas, potentially significantly muting
future business development within the State.

         DCC is concerned that this framework does not adequately account for the realities of
large load project development – including delays outside a customer's direct control – such as
utility construction timelines, equipment procurement lead times, and permitting processes. The
rule does not provide a cure period or an opportunity for the customer to demonstrate progress
before these consequences are initiated. A mandatory reallocation of capacity introduces
significant risk to large load development in Texas and could have a chilling effect on future
business investment in the state.



1
 Data Center Coalition, Comments on Evaluation of Transmission Cost Recovery, Project No. 58484, Item No. 89
(Pub. Util. Comm'n of Tex. 2026), available at
https://interchange.puc.texas.gov/Documents/58484_89_1621024.PDF.


                                                                                                               2
         Given the magnitude of concurrent changes associated with the implementation of
revised large load interconnection processes, DCC recommends the Commission strike §(h) in its
entirety and defer the development of rulemaking on non-utilized capacity to a subsequent
proceeding, after sufficient operational experience has been gained under the proposed batch
framework. In the event the Commission declines to strike §(h), DCC urges that the 80/20
forfeiture structure be replaced with a full refund of any remaining balance after actual costs are
covered, and that meaningful procedural protections be established before any reallocation is
triggered. DCC addresses these concerns in detail in Section II.

2. The 30-Day Deadline to Execute the Interconnection Agreement is an Unrealistic
Timeline

        The proposed rule requires a large load customer to execute an interconnection agreement
within 30 days of completion of the interconnection study. DCC is concerned that this timeline
does not reflect the operational realities of large load project development. Large load projects
involve an intricate sequence of interdependent commitments — including tenant agreements,
construction contracts, equipment procurement, financing arrangements, and power delivery
planning — many of which are negotiated on a tentative basis pending a confirmed
interconnection timeline. Once the interconnection study is complete, the customer must
simultaneously finalize all of these arrangements while executing the interconnection agreement
and satisfying multiple significant financial obligations. The automatic cancellation of an
interconnection request for failure to execute within 30 days is a significant consequence that
may not be warranted in all circumstances. DCC addresses this concern in detail in Section II
and recommends extending the deadline to 60 days, as highlighted in the Commission’s recent
memo.2

3. The Non-Refundable Interconnection Fee Lacks Cost-Causation Justification

        As currently structured, the $50,000 per MW non-refundable interconnection fee under
§(f)(7) is permanently forfeited under all circumstances — including when a project proceeds
exactly as planned and a customer successfully energizes and operates at contracted peak
demand. The rule does not explain what the fee is intended to recover, what specific utility costs
it compensates, how the $50,000 per MW figure was determined, and the process by which the
Commission will ensure that the utility does not overcollect from customers with this fee. This
amount is applied uniformly regardless of actual costs incurred.

       DCC notes that Commission Staff's recent memorandum in Project No. 59142 reflects a
constructive approach to this issue, recommending that financial security escalate in proportion


2
 Public Utility Commission of Texas, Staff Memorandum on Review of ERCOT's Interconnection Processes for
Large Loads, Project No. 59142, Item No. 22 (Pub. Util. Comm'n of Tex. Apr. 12, 2026), available at
https://interchange.puc.texas.gov/Documents/59142_22_1620591.PDF.


                                                                                                           3
 to project development milestones rather than be applied uniformly.3 DCC welcomes this
direction and encourages the Commission to build on it by ensuring that any milestone-based fee
structure is grounded in a transparent demonstration of the actual costs the utility incurs at each
stage of the interconnection process. A milestone-based structure that is not tied to actual costs
simply replaces one unjustified flat charge with several — the underlying cost-causation concern
remains. DCC addresses this in further detail in Section II.

4. The 80/20 Forfeiture Structure is Inconsistent with Cost-Causation Principles

        The 80/20 financial forfeiture structure in §(g)(4) and §(h)(4) results in only 20% of a
customer's remaining financial security — after outstanding actual costs are deducted — being
returned to the customer, with 80% transferred to the interconnecting TSP as an offset to its rate
base. Where the utility has already been made whole for all actual costs incurred, this transfer is
not justified by any demonstrated expense or risk. DCC is also concerned that the rule applies
this same structure to two fundamentally different situations — a customer who has made a
deliberate decision to withdraw under §(g), and a customer who remains committed to their
project but has missed a milestone due to circumstances outside their control under §(h).

         Still, DCC welcomes Commission Staff's recent memorandum in Project No. 59142 as a
constructive step in this direction, recommending that financial security for system upgrades
include only a 20% non-refundable component, with 80% remaining refundable.4 While this
recommendation addresses one component of the broader refundability concern, DCC
encourages the Commission to build on this approach and apply a similar philosophy to the
treatment of withheld financial security more broadly in this rule. DCC addresses this concern in
detail in Section II.

II. Comments on Specific Provisions

        DCC offers the following comments on specific provisions of the proposed rule. These
comments are organized by subsection and are intended to provide the Commission with
specific, actionable recommendations to address the concerns identified in Section I, as well as
additional concerns with specific provisions of the rule. Where DCC proposes changes to rule
text, proposed additions are shown in bold and proposed deletions are shown in strikethrough.




3
  Public Utility Commission of Texas, Staff Memorandum on Review of ERCOT's Interconnection Processes for
Large Loads, Project No. 59142, Item No. 22 (Pub. Util. Comm'n of Tex. Apr. 12, 2026), available at
https://interchange.puc.texas.gov/Documents/59142_22_1620591.PDF.
4
  Public Utility Commission of Texas, Staff Memorandum on Review of ERCOT's Interconnection Processes for
Large Loads, Project No. 59142, Item No. 22 (Pub. Util. Comm'n of Tex. Apr. 12, 2026), available at
https://interchange.puc.texas.gov/Documents/59142_22_1620591.PDF.


                                                                                                            4
    1.​ Grandfathering Projects That Have Already Executed Interconnection Agreements

        DCC urges the Commission to clarify that the requirements established by this rule do
not apply to large load customers that have already executed interconnection agreements and
posted financial security. These projects have already made substantial financial commitments
and operational decisions in reliance on the prior interconnection framework. Applying the new
requirements retroactively to projects that have already completed the interconnection agreement
stage would create significant uncertainty, impose duplicative financial obligations, and
potentially disrupt projects that are in advanced stages of development through no fault of the
customer. DCC recommends that the Commission add explicit grandfathering language to the
rule to protect these projects.



   2.​ Contracted Peak Demand as Competitively Sensitive Information – §(c)(2)

        As noted in Section I, the rule defines competitively sensitive information but explicitly
excludes contracted peak demand from that definition. DCC believes contracted peak demand
should be an explicit exclusion. A customer's contracted peak demand is competitive information
and reflects core business decisions about the scale and timing of their operations. DCC
recommends that the Commission revise §(c)(2) to include contracted peak demand within the
definition of competitively sensitive information, or at minimum to restrict its disclosure beyond
what is necessary for the interconnection process.

       Proposed Language §25.194(c)(2)

       Competitively sensitive information -- Competitively sensitive information includes
       exact site locations, such as parcel identifiers or property boundaries; commercial terms,
       such as pricing or internal development prioritization; proprietary architectural,
       operational, or compute-deployment strategies; and financing structures. Competitively
       sensitive information does not include the identity of a large load customer; general site
       location, such as load zone; requested or contracted peak demand; timing of energization;
       or whether an interconnection request is associated with the same applicant or affiliated
       entities.


   3.​ Site-Related Studies and Engineering Services – §(d)(3) and §(f)(3))

       DCC recognizes the intent of these sections is to evaluate progress on site-related studies
and engineering services to better predict timelines and ensure large load customers utilize their
requested capacity. However, such progress is not always a reliable indicator of a company's




                                                                                                 5
 commitment to completing a project. Numerous factors — many outside the customer's control
— can delay these activities, making them an imperfect measure of project viability.

         The timing of site-related studies and engineering services varies considerably among
large load customers. Currently, energy infrastructure requirements require the longest lead time
and are addressed early in the process, meaning that water, wastewater, or gas studies or
engineering services may not yet have commenced when large load customers request load
studies. Further, many projects would be considered to be well-established before a number of
site-related studies and engineering services would be required. By the time site-related studies
and engineering services have commenced, a project will often have completed several
milestones that strongly indicate it is likely to proceed.

        For these reasons, DCC recommends the Commission strike §(d)(3) and §(f)(3) in their
entirety.



   4.​ State and Local Regulatory Approvals – §(d)(4) and §(f)(4)

        Permitting progress varies significantly across regulatory agencies, with local and state
governments imposing different approval requirements and timelines. Additionally, permits are
often site-specific, and not all data centers require the same set of approvals. In many cases, sites
would be considered to be well-established projects before certain state and local regulatory
approvals have made substantial progress. For these reasons, DCC recommends the Commission
strike §(d)(4) and §(f)(4) in their entirety.



   5.​ Backup Generating Facilities – §(d)(6) and §(f)(6)

         The current language requires the disclosure of information on a large load customer's
backup generating facilities, including the number of units, nameplate capacity, fuel source,
operational characteristics, and the time required for each unit to begin serving the load. DCC
members recognize the importance of providing backup generator information so that
interconnecting utilities can plan for long-term reliability. However, details such as the number
of units, fuel source, and operational capabilities are subject to change — for example, when a
company purchases new equipment or changes providers. Therefore, the rule should allow
flexibility in the level of detail required, ensuring the focus remains on reliability while
minimizing the risk of outdated information. In this context, nameplate capacity is the most
critical data point and is sufficient for reliability planning purposes.

       DCC also urges the Commission to clarify two additional points with respect to backup
generating facilities. First, the disclosure of backup generation information should not be used by


                                                                                                    6
 the interconnecting TDSP as a basis for discriminating against a customer in curtailment
decisions. A customer's possession of backup generation capacity should not result in that
customer being curtailed more quickly or more frequently than other customers. Second, the rule
should make clear that a utility cannot direct or require a customer to operate its backup
generating facilities in a manner that would cause the customer to exceed permitted run hours
under applicable air permits. Compliance with environmental permits is a legal obligation that
cannot be overridden by utility operational directives.

        DCC recommends that §(d)(6) and §(f)(6) be amended to require disclosure of only the
total nameplate capacity of the backup generating facility, and that the rule be clarified to address
the curtailment discrimination and air permit concerns identified above.

       Proposed Language §(d)(6) and §(f)(6)

        (2)​   Backup generating facilities. A large load customer must disclose to the
               interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP whether the customer plans to
               have on-site backup generating facilities. If the large load customer plans to
               have on-site backup generating facilities, the large load customer must also
               disclose the following information:
               (A) the total name plate capacity the number of backup generating units;

               (B) ​ An interconnecting DSP or interconnecting TSP must not use the ​
               ​      disclosure of backup generating facilities under this subsection as a ​
               ​      basis for curtailing a large load customer more quickly or more ​
               ​      frequently than other similarly situated customers. the nameplate
               capacity of each of the backup generating facilities;
               (C)​ An interconnecting DSP or interconnecting TSP must not direct or
                      require a large load customer to operate its backup generating
                      facilities in a manner that would cause the customer to exceed
                      permitted run hours under applicable air permits or other
                      environmental permits. the fuel source and operational characteristics
                      of each of the backup generating facilities, including any run hour
                      limitations and any fuel storage limitations under the existing
                      environmental permits; and
               (D)​ how quickly each of the backup generating facilities can reach their full
                      capacity to serve the load.


   6.​ Study Fee – §(d)(9)

       As currently drafted, the study fee provision establishes a floor — "not less than
$100,000" for projects between 75 MW and 250 MW and "not less than $300,000" for projects

                                                                                                    7
 above 250 MW — but includes no corresponding ceiling. While DCC supports the use of study
fees as a mechanism to demonstrate genuine business interest, the fee should not exceed the
actual costs incurred by the interconnecting TDSP and ERCOT to conduct the interconnection
study. DCC recommends the Commission add ceiling language to ensure that customers are not
required to pay more than the actual cost of the study.

       Proposed Language §(d)(9):

       (A) A large load customer with requested peak demand that is equal to or greater than 75
       MW and less than 250 MW must pay a study fee of not less than $100,000 and not
       more than the actual costs incurred by the interconnecting DSP, the interconnecting
       TSP, and ERCOT to conduct the interconnection study, as applicable.

       (B) A large load customer with requested peak demand that is equal to or greater than
       250 MW must pay a study fee of not less than $300,000 and not more than the actual
       costs incurred by the interconnecting DSP, the interconnecting TSP, and ERCOT to
       conduct the interconnection study.



   7.​ Financial Security on a Dollar Per MW Basis – §(d)(10)

        The $50,000 per megawatt security represents a significant financial commitment made
at an early stage of the interconnection process, when a project's ultimate viability remains
uncertain and many costs have yet to be determined. To the greatest extent possible, this security
should remain refundable until requesting large load customers have greater certainty on project
viability. This protects customers who act in good faith but are unable to proceed for reasons
outside their control. DCC urges the Commission to ensure that this security is not converted into
a permanent forfeiture through its interaction with other financial obligations established later in
the rule.



   8.​ 30-Day Deadline to Execute Interconnection Agreement – §(f)

        The proposed rule requires a large load customer to execute an interconnection agreement
within 30 days of completion of the interconnection study. DCC believes this timeline is wholly
insufficient given the complexity of what must be accomplished during this period.

       Large load projects — and data center projects in particular — involve an intricate
sequence of interdependent commitments that are typically structured around a confirmed
energization date. Customers work backwards from that date to align tenant agreements,
construction contracts, equipment procurement, financing arrangements, and operational


                                                                                                  8
 planning. Many of these commitments are negotiated on a tentative basis pending ERCOT
approval and a confirmed interconnection timeline. Once the interconnection study is complete
and an energization date becomes clearer, the customer must simultaneously finalize and execute
all of these interdependent arrangements — tenant agreements, construction contracts, power
delivery arrangements, and financing — while also negotiating and executing the interconnection
agreement itself with multiple counterparties.

        The interconnection agreement stage also triggers multiple simultaneous financial
obligations, including the non-refundable interconnection fee, financial security for significant
equipment or services, CIAC payment, and financial security for system upgrades. Each of these
obligations requires substantial internal financial planning, capital allocation, and corporate
approval that cannot reasonably be completed within 30 days.

        The consequence of failing to execute within 30 days is automatic cancellation of the
interconnection request — an extreme and irreversible outcome that is disproportionate to what
is in many cases simply a logistical challenge rather than a lack of commitment. DCC notes that
Commission Staff's recent memorandum in Project No. 59142 recommends a 60-day period to
execute interconnection agreements following Batch Zero results — a timeline that reflects a
more realistic assessment of what is operationally feasible.5 DCC recommends that the
Commission adopt a consistent approach in this rule and extend the deadline to execute the
interconnection agreement from 30 days to 60 days to allow sufficient time for all parties to
complete the necessary internal processes, financial arrangements, and commercial commitments
that must be aligned before the interconnection agreement can be executed.

       Proposed Language §(f):

       Not later than 60 30 days after completion of the interconnection study for a large load
       customer, the large load customer must execute an interconnection agreement with the
       interconnecting DSP and, if different from the interconnecting DSP, the interconnecting
       TSP.



    9.​ Non-Refundable Interconnection Fee – §(f)(7)

        As noted in Section I, the $50,000 per MW non-refundable interconnection fee is one of
DCC's principal concerns with the proposed rule. The purpose of financial commitments at this
stage of the interconnection process should be cost recovery — ensuring that the utility is made

Item No. 89 (Pub. Util. Comm'n of Tex. 2026), available at
https://interchange.puc.texas.gov/Documents/58484_89_1621024.PDF.


                                                                                                     9
 whole for actual costs incurred in interconnecting the large load customer. The fee as currently
structured goes well beyond that purpose.

        The rule directs the interconnection fee to be applied as an offset to the interconnecting
TSP's rate base, reflecting an intent to ensure that large load customers contribute to transmission
system costs rather than shifting those costs to other ratepayers. DCC supports that objective.
However, DCC has separately proposed a minimum demand charge in Project No. 58484 as a
more appropriate and precisely calibrated mechanism for achieving that same cost recovery
objective. As DCC noted in its comments in that proceeding, all financial obligations imposed on
large load customers across related rulemakings must be viewed holistically to avoid duplicative
or conflicting cost recovery mechanisms.6 A large load customer subject to both a
non-refundable interconnection fee applied as a rate base offset and an ongoing minimum
demand charge structured around the same transmission system costs would effectively be
paying twice for the same objective. DCC urges the Commission to evaluate these proceedings
together and ensure that the financial obligations established across related rulemakings are
complementary rather than duplicative.

        Beyond the rate base concern, the fee is a flat, uniform charge of $50,000 per MW that is
not tied to any specifically identified or quantifiable cost. The rule provides no explanation of
how this figure was determined or what specific utility costs it is intended to offset. A permanent
non-refundable fee of this magnitude, applied uniformly regardless of actual costs incurred, is
difficult to reconcile with the intent of SB 6, which directs the Commission to establish
interconnection standards in a manner designed to support business development in Texas while
minimizing stranded infrastructure costs.

        DCC is also concerned that the non-refundable fee effectively converts the $50,000 per
MW financial security posted at the intermediate agreement stage — which was nominally
refundable — into a permanent forfeiture at the interconnection agreement stage. Customers who
posted that security with the reasonable expectation that it would be returned if actual costs were
covered will find that expectation defeated. Unlike the CIAC payment under §(f)(9), which
includes a true-up mechanism to adjust for actual versus estimated costs, the interconnection fee
has no equivalent adjustment — it is permanently forfeited regardless of what the utility's actual
costs turn out to be.

         DCC recommends that the Commission restructure the interconnection fee around its
proper purpose — cost recovery. The fee should be applied against actual costs incurred by the
utility to interconnect the large load customer and transferred towards the security needed for
upgrades, and any portion that exceeds those actual costs should be refunded to the customer.
DCC further recommends that the Commission evaluate the interconnection fee in the context of

 the broader financial obligations being considered across related proceedings to ensure that large
load customers are not subject to duplicative cost recovery for the same transmission system

​      Proposed Language §(f)(7):

       Non-refundable interconnection fee. A large load customer must pay an interconnection
       fee in the amount of $50,000 per MW of contracted peak demand. An interconnection fee
       under this subsection is non-refundable. The interconnection fee under this subsection
       shall be applied against actual costs incurred by the interconnecting DSP or the
       interconnecting TSP to interconnect the large load customer. Any portion of the
       interconnection fee that exceeds actual costs incurred shall be refunded to the large load
       customer within 60 days of the completion of the interconnection.

       (A) An interconnecting DSP or an interconnecting TSP must draw on any unused
       financial security that the large load customer posted under an intermediate agreement to
       satisfy the interconnection fee under this subsection.

       (B) An interconnection fee under this subsection must be paid to the interconnecting TSP
       and applied by that TSP as an offset to the interconnecting TSP's rate base in the earlier
       of the interconnecting TSP's next interim rate proceeding or comprehensive rate
       proceeding.

       (C) To the extent the interconnection fee exceeds actual costs incurred, the
       interconnecting TSP must refund the overpayment to the large load customer within 60
       days.



    10.​Contribution in Aid of Construction – (CIAC) §(f)(9), §(g)(5), and §(h)(5)

        As with the non-refundable interconnection fee discussed above, DCC's comments on
CIAC are grounded in the principle that financial obligations imposed on large load customers
should be tied to actual, quantifiable utility costs and should not result in permanent forfeitures
that go beyond legitimate cost recovery. DCC supports the concept of CIAC as a cost recovery
mechanism — requiring large load customers to pay the direct costs of infrastructure built
specifically to serve their load is consistent with cost-causation principles and DCC members are
prepared to meet that obligation. However, the CIAC provisions as currently drafted raise two
concerns that DCC urges the Commission to address.




                                                                                                 11
 A)​ Payment Timeline

           The rule requires a large load customer to pay CIAC no later than the date the
   interconnection agreement is executed. As discussed in the context of the 30-day deadline
   to execute the interconnection agreement, the interconnection agreement stage requires
   the simultaneous alignment of multiple significant financial obligations — the
   interconnection fee, financial security for equipment and services, financial security for
   system upgrades, and CIAC — all within a compressed timeframe. CIAC payments for
   large load projects can represent tens or hundreds of millions of dollars. Requiring
   payment on the date the interconnection agreement is executed, without any additional
   time to arrange financing or obtain necessary corporate approvals, is not workable in
   practice. DCC recommends that the rule allow at least 60 days after execution of the
   interconnection agreement for CIAC payment.

B)​ Refundability

            Sections §(g)(5) and §(h)(5) both provide that CIAC is not refundable under any
   circumstances. DCC believes this is too absolute. Consistent with the cost-causation and
   cost-recovery principles that DCC has advocated throughout this proceeding, CIAC
   should be refundable to the extent that the utility's actual costs are fully covered and a
   remaining balance exists. If the utility has been made whole for all actual direct
   interconnection costs attributable to the large load customer, there is no cost-recovery
   justification for retaining any excess. Permanently withholding funds beyond what is
   necessary to cover actual costs goes beyond cost recovery and is inconsistent with the
   intent of SB 6, which directs the Commission to establish interconnection standards in a
   manner designed to support business development in Texas.

          DCC recommends that §(g)(5) and §(h)(5) be amended to provide that CIAC is
   refundable to the extent that the utility's actual direct interconnection costs are fully
   covered and a remaining balance exists.

   Proposed Language §(f)(9):

   (9) Contribution in aid of construction (CIAC). A large load customer must pay all direct
   interconnection costs through CIAC, with no standard or other allowance offered to offset
   the customer's CIAC payments. A large load customer must pay CIAC not later than the
   date that the interconnection agreement is executed 60 days after the date that the
   interconnection agreement is executed.

   Proposed Language §(g)(5) and §(h)(5):




                                                                                               12
        CIAC is not refundable. CIAC is not refundable except to the extent that the utility's
       actual direct interconnection costs attributable to the large load customer are fully
       covered, in which case the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP must
       refund any remaining balance to the large load customer within 60 days.



   11.​Withdrawal of Requested or Contracted Peak Demand – §(g)

        As noted in Section I, DCC's principal concern with §(g) centers on the financial
forfeiture structure triggered upon withdrawal.

   A)​ 80/20 Forfeiture Structure – §(g)(4)

                As noted in Section I, the 80/20 financial forfeiture structure is one of DCC's
       principal concerns with the proposed rule. After outstanding actual costs are deducted
       from a customer's posted financial security, only 20% of the remaining balance is
       returned to the customer — with 80% transferred to the interconnecting TSP as an offset
       to its rate base. Because the utility has already been made whole for all actual costs
       incurred, this transfer represents a financial benefit to the TSP that bears no connection to
       any demonstrated expense or risk associated with the customer's project.

                The purpose of financial security should be cost recovery. Once the utility has
       been made whole for all actual costs incurred, the remaining balance of a customer's
       financial security has served its intended purpose and should be returned to the customer
       in full. DCC urges the Commission to amend §(g)(4) to require that the full remaining
       balance of a customer's financial security, after deduction of actual outstanding costs, be
       refunded to the customer. If the Commission believes some level of forfeiture is
       warranted as a deterrent against speculative interconnection requests, DCC recommends
       that any such forfeiture be explicitly tied to a demonstrated, quantifiable harm to the
       utility or to ratepayers rather than serving as a transfer to the TSP's rate base. DCC also
       reiterates its position, as discussed in the context of §(f)(9) above, that CIAC should be
       refundable to the extent that the utility's actual direct interconnection costs are fully
       covered and a remaining balance exists.

       Proposed Language §(g)(3) and §(g)(4):

       (3) After applying the large load customer's financial security to any outstanding amounts
       owed, the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP must refund 20% 100% of the
       balance to the large load customer within 60 days.

       (4) After applying the financial security to any outstanding amounts owed and refunding
       20% of the balance, the remaining 80% of the balance must be paid to the interconnecting


                                                                                                  13
        TSP and applied by that TSP as an offset to the interconnecting TSP's rate base in the
       earlier of the interconnecting TSP's next interim rate proceeding or comprehensive rate
       proceeding.



   12.​Non-Utilized Capacity – §(h)

        As noted in Section I, the non-utilized capacity provisions in §(h) represent one of DCC's
most significant concerns with the proposed rule. Together, the six-month milestone trigger, the
mandatory capacity reallocation, and the 80/20 financial forfeiture establish a sequence of
consequences that are disproportionate, difficult to reverse, and that do not distinguish between
customers who have abandoned their projects and those who remain fully committed but face
delays outside their control. For the reasons set forth below, DCC recommends that §(h) be
struck in its entirety and that the Commission defer development of non-utilized capacity rules to
a subsequent proceeding.



   A)​ Six-Month Milestone Trigger – §(h)(1)

               The rule requires the interconnecting TDSP to notify ERCOT of a large load
       customer's non-utilized capacity not later than 30 days after the customer fails, by six
       months, to satisfy a milestone in its schedule for phased energization. Within 60 days of
       that notification, the TDSP must initiate draw-down on the customer's posted financial
       security for costs incurred, including equipment that cannot be canceled, construction that
       has commenced, and services that have been initiated. DCC believes this six-month
       threshold is unreasonably short and does not reflect the operational realities of large load
       project development.

                As a threshold matter, the rule does not adequately define what it means to "fail"
       to satisfy an energization milestone. The phased energization schedule is established
       early in the interconnection process, at a time when many project variables remain
       uncertain. Whether a customer has "failed" to meet a milestone is not always clear —
       projects ramp up in phases, timelines shift for reasons outside anyone's control, and
       partial progress toward a milestone may not constitute "failure" in any meaningful sense.
       The rule provides no guidance on how milestone compliance is measured, who makes
       that determination, or what standard of review applies. This ambiguity creates significant
       legal and operational uncertainty for large load customers and their lenders, tenants, and
       construction partners who are making commitments based on the interconnection
       timeline.




                                                                                                 14
          A critical distinction that the rule entirely fails to make is the difference between a
customer's failure to reach contracted peak demand and genuine non-utilization of
allocated capacity. Modern data centers are increasingly designed and operated with
energy and water efficiency as a primary objective. A customer operating an efficient
facility may never reach their contracted peak demand precisely because they are
achieving more with less. A large load customer may have fully constructed their facility,
be actively running compute workloads, operating cooling systems, and consuming
meaningful amounts of energy — yet not reach their contracted peak demand because
they are operating efficiently. To treat efficient operation as equivalent to non-utilization
fundamentally misunderstands how modern data centers operate and would create a
perverse incentive structure that penalizes efficiency and rewards wasteful energy
consumption. This fundamental conceptual flaw in the non-utilized capacity framework
is one of the principal reasons DCC believes §(h) cannot be adequately remedied through
amendments alone and should be struck in its entirety and reconsidered in a subsequent
proceeding.

        The rule also makes no distinction based on the cause of the delay. A milestone
miss attributable to a TDSP construction delay, an ERCOT process issue, a natural
disaster, a global supply chain disruption, or any other factor entirely outside the
customer's control triggers the same consequences as a miss caused by the customer's
own failure to perform. This is fundamentally inequitable. A customer acting in complete
good faith could miss a milestone by six months for reasons directly attributable to the
TDSP or ERCOT itself and still face the permanent loss of their capacity position and the
majority of their posted financial security — an outcome that is not consistent with the
Commission's goal of supporting business development in Texas and that cannot be
justified by any analysis of actual utility risk or ratepayer exposure.

        The stakes here cannot be overstated. By the time a capacity reallocation is
triggered under §(h), a large load customer will have made substantial and largely
irreversible investments in site development, permitting, infrastructure planning, tenant
commitments, equipment procurement, and construction — investments that could
collectively represent billions of dollars. The mandatory and automatic reallocation of
capacity at that stage does not simply impose a financial loss — it threatens to strand
those investments entirely, potentially rendering years of development work worthless.
Under such risk conditions, the non-utilized capacity framework as currently drafted
could significantly deter future large load investment in Texas, undermining the very
business development goals that SB 6 and this rulemaking are intended to advance.




                                                                                             15
 B)​ 80/20 Forfeiture Structure – §(h)(4)

          The 80/20 forfeiture structure in §(h)(4) compounds the problems described above
   by applying the same financial consequences to a customer who has not withdrawn and
   remains fully committed to their project as it does to a customer who has voluntarily
   walked away. A customer subject to §(h) has posted substantial financial security,
   executed agreements with the utility, and committed to completing their project — and in
   many cases has made billions of dollars in additional investments in reliance on that
   interconnection. The sole basis for triggering the forfeiture is a six-month milestone miss
   — a threshold that is unreasonably short, poorly defined, and does not account for delays
   outside the customer's control, including delays directly attributable to the TDSP or
   ERCOT.

           For the same reasons articulated in the context of §(g)(4) above, the full
   remaining balance of a customer's financial security, after deduction of actual outstanding
   costs, should be refunded to the customer. Applying the same 80/20 forfeiture to a
   committed customer experiencing an unavoidable delay as to one who has abandoned
   their project is inequitable and inconsistent with the cost-causation principles that should
   govern financial security in this rule. DCC also reiterates its position that CIAC should be
   refundable to the extent that the utility's actual direct interconnection costs are fully
   covered and a remaining balance exists.



C)​ Mandatory Capacity Reallocation – §(h)(6)

           Section §(h)(6) provides that ERCOT must reallocate non-utilized capacity once
   notified under §(h)(1). The language is mandatory — there is no discretion, no cure
   period, no opportunity for the customer to demonstrate progress, and no requirement for
   mutual consent between the TDSP and the customer before reallocation is triggered.

           The loss of capacity is the most severe consequence in this rule because it is
   effectively permanent. A customer whose capacity is reallocated does not simply
   experience a financial loss — they lose their position in the interconnection queue
   entirely and must restart the process, repost security, and potentially wait years before
   they can energize. For a project that has already invested substantially — potentially
   billions of dollars — in site development, permitting, infrastructure planning, tenant
   agreements, equipment procurement, and construction, mandatory capacity reallocation
   can effectively end the project regardless of the customer's intent or ability to proceed.
   The prospect of this outcome, triggered automatically by a vaguely defined milestone
   miss that may be entirely outside the customer's control, creates an investment risk
   profile that could significantly deter future large load development in Texas and


                                                                                                16
        undermine the state's position as a premier destination for data center and other large load
       investment.

Recommendation — Strike §(h) in Its Entirety

        DCC recommends that the Commission strike §(h) in its entirety from this rulemaking
and defer the development of non-utilized capacity rules to a subsequent proceeding. Given the
magnitude of concurrent changes associated with the implementation of revised large load
interconnection processes, including the Batch Zero Study Process, the non-utilized capacity
framework should not be finalized until sufficient operational experience has been gained under
the new interconnection framework and a more stable implementation cadence has been
established.²

        The framework as currently drafted is fundamentally incompatible with the realities of
large load development. The milestone definitions are ambiguous, the triggers are unreasonably
short, the consequences are irreversible, and the 80/20 financial forfeiture structure penalizes
committed customers who face unavoidable delays in the same manner as those who have
abandoned their projects entirely. The rule makes no meaningful distinction between customers
who have genuinely abandoned their projects and those who are actively developing them —
operating facilities, running compute workloads, consuming energy efficiently, and investing
billions of dollars in infrastructure — but face delays outside their control. The potential for
billions of dollars in stranded investment, triggered by a vaguely defined milestone miss that
may be entirely attributable to the utility or ERCOT, creates an unacceptable level of risk that
could significantly deter future large load investment in Texas. A framework that simultaneously
imposes the 80/20 financial forfeiture and mandatory capacity reallocation on committed
customers facing unavoidable delays is not consistent with the Commission's goal of supporting
business development in Texas, is not grounded in cost-causation principles, and is not justified
by any analysis of actual utility risk or ratepayer exposure.

        Deferral would allow the Commission to develop non-utilized capacity rules with the
benefit of real-world experience under the Batch Zero framework, informed stakeholder input,
and a clearer understanding of how phased energization schedules actually operate in practice —
including the critical distinction between genuine non-utilization and efficient operation that the
current framework entirely ignores. DCC stands ready to engage constructively in that
subsequent proceeding to help develop a non-utilized capacity framework that is workable,
equitable, and consistent with the cost-causation principles that underpin utility regulation in
Texas.




                                                                                                 17
 III. Conclusion

        Data centers are critical to our modern economy and daily lives, and our industry is eager
to contribute to solutions that advance an affordable and reliable grid that continues to support
economic growth in Texas.DCC's comments in this proceeding have been guided by a consistent
and principled framework: financial obligations imposed on large load customers should be
proportionate, transparent, and grounded in actual utility costs consistent with the intent of SB 6
and the cost-causation principles that underpin utility regulation in Texas.

        DCC also reiterates its recommendation that the Commission evaluate the financial
obligations established in this rule holistically and in the context of the broader regulatory
requirements being considered across related proceedings, including Project No. 58484, to
ensure that Texas remains a competitive destination for the large load investment that is essential
to the state's economic growth and long-term energy security. DCC is committed to being a
collaborative partner and a part of the solution to meeting Texas's energy demand and reliability
goals, and we look forward to continued engagement with the Commission, utilities, customers,
and other stakeholders in Texas as this important rulemaking is finalized.

   8. 30-Day Deadline to Execute Interconnection Agreement - §(f)

       The proposed rule requires a large load customer to execute an interconnection agreement
within 30 days of completion of the interconnection study. DCC believes this timeline is wholly
insufficient given the complexity of what must be accomplished during this period.

       Large load projects - and data center proj ects in particular - involve an intricate
sequence of interdependent commitments that are typically structured around a confirmed
energization date. Customers work backwards from that date to align tenant agreements,
construction contracts, equipment procurement, financing arrangements, and operational

approval and a confirmed interconnection timeline. Once the interconnection study is complete
and an energization date becomes clearer, the customer must simultaneously finalize and execute
all of these interdependent arrangements - tenant agreements, construction contracts, power
delivery arrangements, and financing - while also negotiating and executing the interconnection
agreement itself with multiple counterparties.

obligations, including the non-refundable interconnection fee, financial security for significant
equipment or services, CIAC payment, and financial security for system upgrades. Each of these
obligations requires substantial internal financial planning, capital allocation, and corporate
approval that cannot reasonably be completed within 30 days.

       The consequence of failing to execute within 30 days is automatic cancellation of the
interconnection request - an extreme and irreversible outcome that is disproportionate to what
is in many cases simply a logistical challenge rather than a lack of commitment. DCC notes that

execute interconnection agreements following Batch Zero results - a timeline that reflects a
more realistic assessment of what is operationally feasible.5 DCC recommends that the

   12. Non-Utilized Capacity - §(h)

        As noted in Section I, the non-utilized capacity provisions in §(h) represent one of DCC's
most significant concerns with the proposed rule. Together, the six-month milestone trigger, the
mandatory capacity reallocation, and the 80/20 financial forfeiture establish a sequence of
consequences that are disproportionate, difficult to reverse, and that do not distinguish between
customers who have abandoned their projects and those who remain fully committed but face
delays outside their control. For the reasons set forth below, DCC recommends that §(h) be
struck in its entirety and that the Commission defer development of non-utilized capacity rules to
a subsequent proceeding.



   A) Six-Month Milestone Trigger - §(h)(1)

               The rule requires the interconnecting TDSP to notify ERCOT of a large load
       customer's non-utilized capacity not later than 30 days after the customer fails, by six
       months, to satisfy a milestone in its schedule for phased energization. Within 60 days of
       that notification, the TDSP must initiate draw-down on the customer's posted financial
       security for costs incurred, including equipment that cannot be canceled, construction that
       has commenced, and services that have been initiated. DCC believes this six-month
       threshold is unreasonably short and does not reflect the operational realities of large load
       proj ect development.

               As a threshold matter, the rule does not adequately define what it means to "fail"
       to satisfy an energization milestone. The phased energization schedule is established
       early in the interconnection process, at a time when many project variables remain
       uncertain. Whether a customer has "failed" to meet a milestone is not always clear -
       projects ramp up in phases, timelines shift for reasons outside anyone's control, and
       partial progress toward a milestone may not constitute "failure" in any meaningful sense.
       The rule provides no guidance on how milestone compliance is measured, who makes
       that determination, or what standard of review applies. This ambiguity creates significant
       legal and operational uncertainty for large load customers and their lenders, tenants, and
       construction partners who are making commitments based on the interconnection
       timeline.




                                                                                                 14
          A critical distinction that the rule entirely fails to make is the difference between a
customer's failure to reach contracted peak demand and genuine non-utilization of
allocated capacity. Modern data centers are increasingly designed and operated with
energy and water efficiency as a primary obj ective. A customer operating an efficient
facility may never reach their contracted peak demand precisely because they are
achieving more with less. A large load customer may have fully constructed their facility,
be actively running compute workloads, operating cooling systems, and consuming
meaningful amounts of energy - yet not reach their contracted peak demand because
they are operating efficiently. To treat efficient operation as equivalent to non-utilization
fundamentally misunderstands how modern data centers operate and would create a
perverse incentive structure that penalizes efficiency and rewards wasteful energy
consumption. This fundamental conceptual flaw in the non-utilized capacity framework
is one of the principal reasons DCC believes §(h) cannot be adequately remedied through
amendments alone and should be struck in its entirety and reconsidered in a subsequent
proceeding.

        The rule also makes no distinction based on the cause of the delay. A milestone
miss attributable to a TDSP construction delay, an ERCOT process issue, a natural
disaster, a global supply chain disruption, or any other factor entirely outside the
customer's control triggers the same consequences as a miss caused by the customer's
own failure to perform. This is fundamentally inequitable. A customer acting in complete
good faith could miss a milestone by six months for reasons directly attributable to the
 TDSP or ERCOT itself and still face the permanent loss of their capacity position and the
majority of their posted financial security - an outcome that is not consistent with the
 Commission's goal of supporting business development in Texas and that cannot be
justified by any analysis of actual utility risk or ratepayer exposure.

        The stakes here cannot be overstated. By the time a capacity reallocation is
triggered under §(h), a large load customer will have made substantial and largely
irreversible investments in site development, permitting, infrastructure planning, tenant
commitments, equipment procurement, and construction - investments that could
collectively represent billions of dollars. The mandatory and automatic reallocation of
capacity at that stage does not simply impose a financial loss - it threatens to strand
those investments entirely, potentially rendering years of development work worthless.
Under such risk conditions, the non-utilized capacity framework as currently drafted
could significantly deter future large load investment in Texas, undermining the very
business development goals that SB 6 and this rulemaking are intended to advance.

 B) 80/20 Forfeiture Structure - §(h)(4)

          The 80/20 forfeiture structure in §(h)(4) compounds the problems described above
   by applying the same financial consequences to a customer who has not withdrawn and
   remains fully committed to their proj ect as it does to a customer who has voluntarily
   walked away. A customer subject to §(h) has posted substantial financial security,
   executed agreements with the utility, and committed to completing their project - and in
   many cases has made billions of dollars in additional investments in reliance on that
   interconnection. The sole basis for triggering the forfeiture is a six-month milestone miss
   - a threshold that is unreasonably short, poorly defined, and does not account for delays
   outside the customer's control, including delays directly attributable to the TDSP or
   ERCOT.
          For the same reasons articulated in the context of §(g)(4) above, the full
   remaining balance of a customer's financial security, after deduction of actual outstanding
   costs, should be refunded to the customer. Applying the same 80/20 forfeiture to a
   committed customer experiencing an unavoidable delay as to one who has abandoned
   their project is inequitable and inconsistent with the cost-causation principles that should
   govern financial security in this rule. DCC also reiterates its position that CIAC should be
   refundable to the extent that the utility's actual direct interconnection costs are fully
   covered and a remaining balance exists.



C) Mandatory Capacity Reallocation - §(h)(6)

           Section §(h)(6) provides that ERCOT must reallocate non-utilized capacity once
   notified under §(h)(1). The language is mandatory - there is no discretion, no cure
   period, no opportunity for the customer to demonstrate progress, and no requirement for
   mutual consent between the TDSP and the customer before reallocation is triggered.

           The loss of capacity is the most severe consequence in this rule because it is
   effectively permanent. A customer whose capacity is reallocated does not simply
   experience a financial loss - they lose their position in the interconnection queue
   entirely and must restart the process, repost security, and potentially wait years before
   they can energize. For a project that has already invested substantially - potentially
   billions of dollars - in site development, permitting, infrastructure planning, tenant
   agreements, equipment procurement, and construction, mandatory capacity reallocation
   can effectively end the project regardless of the customer's intent or ability to proceed.
   The prospect of this outcome, triggered automatically by a vaguely defined milestone
   miss that may be entirely outside the customer's control, creates an investment risk
   profile that could significantly deter future large load development in Texas and

Recommendation - Strike §(h) in Its Entirety

        DCC recommends that the Commission strike §( h ) in its entirety from this rulemaking
and defer the development of non-utilized capacity rules to a subsequent proceeding. Given the
magnitude of concurrent changes associated with the implementation of revised large load
interconnection processes, including the Batch Zero Study Process, the non-utilized capacity
framework should not be finalized until sufficient operational experience has been gained under
the new interconnection framework and a more stable implementation cadence has been
established. 2

        The framework as currently drafted is fundamentally incompatible with the realities of
large load development. The milestone definitions are ambiguous, the triggers are unreasonably
short, the consequences are irreversible, and the 80/20 financial forfeiture structure penalizes
committed customers who face unavoidable delays in the same manner as those who have
abandoned their projects entirely. The rule makes no meaningful distinction between customers
who have genuinely abandoned their proj ects and those who are actively developing them -
operating facilities, running compute workloads, consuming energy efficiently, and investing
billions of dollars in infrastructure - but face delays outside their control. The potential for
billions of dollars in stranded investment, triggered by a vaguely defined milestone miss that
may be entirely attributable to the utility or ERCOT, creates an unacceptable level of risk that
could significantly deter future large load investment in Texas. A framework that simultaneously
imposes the 80/20 financial forfeiture and mandatory capacity reallocation on committed
customers facing unavoidable delays is not consistent with the Commission's goal of supporting
business development in Texas, is not grounded in cost-causation principles, and is not justified
by any analysis of actual utility risk or ratepayer exposure.

        Deferral would allow the Commission to develop non-utilized capacity rules with the
benefit of real-world experience under the Batch Zero framework, informed stakeholder input,
and a clearer understanding of how phased energization schedules actually operate in practice -
including the critical distinction between genuine non-utilization and efficient operation that the
current framework entirely ignores. DCC stands ready to engage constructively in that
subsequent proceeding to help develop a non-utilized capacity framework that is workable,
equitable, and consistent with the cost-causation principles that underpin utility regulation in
Texas.
